blocks.text: Parts of the male reproductive system

items: Gonads (testes): two oval testes, about 3 to 5 cm long and 2 to 3 cm wide, in a skin pouch, the scrotum, outside the abdomen. Each is made of highly coiled seminiferous tubules whose wall, the germinal epithelium, has germline cells, which make sperms (spermatozoa) by meiosis, and Sertoli cells, which nourish them.

Accessory ducts: from the seminiferous tubules sperm enter the rete testis, then the long coiled epididymis, where they stay non-motile for at least 18 hours before becoming motile; then the vas deferens, which passes into the abdomen through the inguinal canal and joins the duct of a seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct. The two ejaculatory ducts pass through the prostate and open into the urethra, which comes from the bladder and opens through the penis.

Accessory glands, which add fluids to sperm to form semen: two seminal vesicles (a fructose-rich fluid that gives the sperm energy); the prostate gland below the bladder (soft and spongy, about 60% of the semen); and two bulbourethral glands (a clear fluid that lubricates the urethra and gives a protective neutral environment).
Copulatory organ (penis): contains the urethra, erectile tissue, an artery and two veins.

blocks.title: Why the testes are outside
blocks.text: The testes form inside the abdomen and descend into the scrotum shortly before birth. The scrotum keeps them at about 34 C, slightly below the core temperature of 37 C, which sperm development needs.

blocks.alt: Left: a schematic front view of the male reproductive organs: the urinary bladder, the prostate gland below it, two seminal vesicles, two small bulbourethral glands, the urethra running down through the penis, and two testes in the scrotum, each with an epididymis and a vas deferens that loops up to join the urethra. Right: a seminiferous tubule in section, with germline cells at the wall, Sertoli cells, sperm tails in the central lumen and Leydig cells between tubules.
blocks.caption: Male reproductive system and a cross-section of a testis (original diagram after Figure 17.1).
blocks.long_description: Each testis, in the scrotum at about 34 C, is made of coiled seminiferous tubules whose germline cells make sperm by meiosis while Sertoli cells nourish them; Leydig cells between the tubules make testosterone. Sperm pass through the rete testis to the epididymis, where after at least 18 hours they become motile, then along the vas deferens, which joins the duct of a seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct; the ejaculatory ducts pass through the prostate and open into the urethra, which runs through the penis. The seminal vesicles add a fructose-rich fluid, the prostate about 60% of the semen, and the bulbourethral glands a clear lubricating fluid.

blocks.text: Spermatogenesis is the formation of sperm in the seminiferous tubules. Germline cells (2n) in the tubule wall divide by mitosis; some become spermatogonia (2n) and others stay as germline cells. Spermatogonia form primary spermatocytes (2n), which move towards the lumen. Each primary spermatocyte divides by meiosis I into two secondary spermatocytes (1n), which quickly undergo meiosis II to give spermatids (1n): one spermatogonium gives four spermatids, each maturing into an elongated sperm.

A sperm has a head, a midpiece and a tail. The head holds the genetic material, and about two thirds of it is covered by the acrosome, a cap formed mainly from the Golgi body, with enzymes that help the sperm fertilize the ovum. The midpiece contains mitochondria and a centriole; the tail is made of microtubules (the axial filament) arising from that centriole. Mature sperm in the lumen are non-motile and reach the epididymis carried by fluid from the Sertoli cells; they gain motility there.

blocks.alt: Left: spermatogenesis as a chain of cells: germline cell (2n), spermatogonium (2n), primary spermatocyte (2n), meiosis I to two secondary spermatocytes (1n), meiosis II to four spermatids (1n) and four sperms, with a sperm's head, acrosome, midpiece and tail shown below. Right: oogenesis: oogonium (2n), primary oocyte (2n) stopped in prophase I until puberty, meiosis I to a secondary oocyte and a first polar body, and, if a sperm enters, meiosis II to one ovum and a second polar body.
blocks.caption: Spermatogenesis and the structure of a sperm (original diagram after Figure 17.2).
blocks.long_description: In the testis, germline cells divide by mitosis; some become spermatogonia, which form primary spermatocytes; each primary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis I to form two secondary spermatocytes and meiosis II to form four spermatids, which mature into sperms with a head (nucleus and acrosome), a midpiece (mitochondria and a centriole) and a tail. In the ovary, oogonia form primary oocytes before birth, which stop in prophase I; from puberty one at a time completes meiosis I to give a large secondary oocyte and a small first polar body; the secondary oocyte, stopped in metaphase II, is released at ovulation and completes meiosis II only if a sperm enters, giving one ovum and a second polar body.

blocks.text: Spermatogenesis is controlled by hormones of the hypothalamus and pituitary. The hypothalamus releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which makes the anterior pituitary release FSH and LH. FSH stimulates the seminiferous tubules to carry out spermatogenesis. LH stimulates the Leydig cells, in the interstitial tissue between the tubules, to secrete testosterone, which stimulates the germinal epithelium and maintains male secondary sexual characteristics. FSH also makes the Sertoli cells release inhibin, a peptide hormone that inhibits further FSH secretion, and testosterone inhibits the release of LH and GnRH.

blocks.alt: A flow chart. The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which makes the anterior pituitary release FSH and LH. FSH acts on Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules, leading to spermatogenesis; LH acts on Leydig cells between the tubules, which secrete testosterone for the germinal epithelium and male traits. Dashed arrows show negative feedback: inhibin from Sertoli cells stops FSH, and testosterone stops LH and GnRH.
blocks.caption: Hormonal control of the male reproductive system (original diagram after Figure 17.3).
blocks.long_description: GnRH from the hypothalamus makes the anterior pituitary release FSH and LH. FSH stimulates the seminiferous tubules (through the Sertoli cells) to carry out spermatogenesis; LH stimulates the Leydig cells to secrete testosterone, which supports the germinal epithelium and maintains male secondary sexual characteristics. Sertoli cells stimulated by FSH release inhibin, which inhibits further FSH secretion, and testosterone inhibits the release of LH and GnRH: two negative feedback loops.

blocks.prompt: List, in order, the structures a sperm passes from the seminiferous tubule to the outside.
blocks.explanation: Seminiferous tubule, rete testis, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct (through the prostate), urethra (in the penis).

items: Testes (in the scrotum, 34 C): seminiferous tubules with germline and Sertoli cells; Leydig cells make testosterone.
Ducts: rete testis, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra; glands: seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral.
One spermatogonium gives four sperms; GnRH, FSH (sperm), LH (testosterone), inhibin and testosterone feed back.
